1.title: ServiceAccounts, Authentication, Authorization and Admission Control
1.text: Welcome to Module eleven: Service Accounts, Authentication, Authorization and Admission Control. It covers the exam area Application Environment, Configuration and Security. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, and every task was run on a real cluster, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do three things. Understand authentication, authorization and admission control. Understand Service Accounts. Practice with seven hands-on labs worth forty-six points.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Exam area: Application Environment, Configuration and Security (twenty-five percent). Practice in this module: seven labs, forty-six points, about forty-seven minutes. Exam format: performance-based tasks in a live terminal, scored on the final cluster state. Validated on: Kubernetes version one point thirty-seven point zero.

1.title: Every API request passes three gates
1.text: Every A P I request passes three gates. The figure shows this: The three gates of the A P I server. Exam tip: A four hundred three Forbidden is authorization (R back), a four hundred one is authentication, and an admission error names the policy.

1.title: Every API request passes three gates, continued
1.text: Every A P I request passes three gates. When kube control or a Pod calls the A P I server, the request is checked in order. one. Authentication. Question: who are you? Typical answer: a client certificate, a bearer token (a Service Account token), an O I D C token. If it fails: four hundred one Unauthorized. two. Authorization. Question: may you do this to this object? Typical answer: R back rules (a Role or Cluster Role bound to you). If it fails: four hundred three Forbidden. three. Admission control. Question: is this object acceptable (and may it be changed)? Typical answer: mutating and validating admission: defaults, quotas, Pod Security. If it fails: an error naming the policy. Authentication and authorization decide about the caller; admission decides about the object. Admission runs only for create, update and delete, and a request that fails authorization never reaches it.

1.title: Authentication: users and ServiceAccounts
1.text: Authentication: users and Service Accounts. Kubernetes has no user objects. A person is whoever the cluster's authenticator recognizes (a certificate with C N jane, an O I D C identity). Pods authenticate with a Service Account, an object in a namespace. Its identity is system serviceaccount namespace name. kube control auth whoami shows who the cluster thinks you are.

1.title: ServiceAccounts in Pods
1.text: Service Accounts in Pods. Every namespace has a default Service Account, and a Pod without service Account Name uses it. A Pod's containers get a short-lived token through a projected volume at slash var slash run slash secrets slash Kubernetes dot io slash serviceaccount or (files token, ca dot crt, namespace ). Code in the Pod uses it to call the A P I server at H T T P S colon slash slash Kubernetes dot default dot svc. Exam tip: Set automount Service Account Token false on Pods that never call the A P I.

1.title: ServiceAccounts in Pods, continued
1.text: Service Accounts in Pods. spec dot service Account Name. the identity of the Pod (cannot change on a running Pod). spec dot automount Service Account Token false. the Pod gets no token; set it on Pods that never call the A P I. service Account dot automount Service Account Token false. the same default for every Pod using that Service Account (a Pod can override). image Pull Secrets on a Service Account. every Pod using it can pull from that registry.

1.title: ServiceAccounts in Pods, continued
1.text: Service Accounts in Pods. Tokens on demand. kube control create token app sa dash n auth the duration flag set to two hours prints a token that expires (default one hour). Use it with the token flag or in an Authorization Bearer... header. These tokens are signed J W Ts: the middle part decodes to the sub, iat and exp claims.

1.title: Authorization with RBAC
1.text: Authorization with R back. R back answers "who may do what". It has four objects. Role. Scope: one namespace. Purpose: a list of rules: verbs on resources. Cluster Role. Scope: whole cluster. Purpose: the same, plus non-namespaced resources (nodes) and cluster-wide use. Role Binding. Scope: one namespace. Purpose: gives a Role or a Cluster Role to subjects in that namespace. Cluster Role Binding. Scope: whole cluster. Purpose: gives a Cluster Role to subjects in every namespace. Exam tip: A Role Binding that points at a Cluster Role grants the rules in one namespace only; test with kube control auth can i.

1.title: Authorization with RBAC, continued
1.text: Authorization with R back. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Authorization with RBAC, continued
1.text: Authorization with R back. A Role Binding that points at a Cluster Role is the neat way to reuse a rule set in one namespace: the permissions apply only in the binding's namespace. Verbs: get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete, deletecollection. A subject is a User, a Group or a Service Account ( the serviceaccount flag set to namespace name, the user flag set to jane, the group flag set to devs ). Check access with can i.

1.title: Authorization with RBAC, continued
1.text: Authorization with R back. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Authorization with RBAC, continued
1.text: Authorization with R back. R back is additive: there are no deny rules. If you cannot reach something, add a rule; to remove access, delete the binding. The role Ref of a binding cannot be edited: delete and recreate it.

1.title: A 403 inside a Pod
1.text: A four hundred three inside a Pod. A Pod that calls the A P I and gets four hundred three Forbidden runs under a Service Account without the right rule. The error text names the user and the verb, for example pods is forbidden User system serviceaccount auth app sa cannot list resource pods in the namespace auth. Create the Role (the exact verb and resource) and the Role Binding to that Service Account; the Pod does not need to restart.

1.title: Admission control
1.text: Admission control. After authorization, admission controllers can change (mutating) or refuse (validating) the object. Several are on by default, and you have already met three. Service Account. What it does: puts the default Service Account and the token volume into Pods. Where you met it: this module. Limit Ranger. What it does: fills in default requests and limits, rejects values outside min and max. Where you met it: Module ten. Resource Quota. What it does: rejects objects that would exceed the namespace quota. Where you met it: Module ten. Namespace Lifecycle. What it does: rejects objects in a namespace that is being deleted. Exam tip: The Pod Security labels enforce, warn and audit use the levels privileged, baseline and restricted.

1.title: Admission control, continued
1.text: Admission control. Pod Security. What it does: enforces the Pod Security Standards by namespace label. Where you met it: below. Validating Admission Policy. What it does: your own validation rules in sell, without running a webhook. Where you met it: below. webhooks. What it does: Mutating Webhook Configuration, Validating Webhook Configuration call a service you run. Where you met it: operators and policy engines.

1.title: Pod Security Admission
1.text: Pod Security Admission. The three Pod Security Standards are privileged (no restrictions), baseline (blocks the known privilege escalations: privileged containers, host namespaces, host paths, extra capabilities) and restricted (current hardening best practice: non-root user, no privilege escalation, drop all capabilities, a sec comp profile). A namespace label picks the mode and the level. pod security dot Kubernetes dot io slash enforce baseline. Mode: enforce. Effect: violating Pods are rejected. pod security dot Kubernetes dot io slash warn baseline. Mode: warn. Effect: the user gets a warning, the Pod is created. pod security dot Kubernetes dot io slash audit baseline. Mode: audit. Effect: an audit-log annotation, the Pod is created.

1.title: Pod Security Admission, continued
1.text: Pod Security Admission. The example is on the screen; read it line by line when you study.

1.title: Pod Security Admission, continued
1.text: Pod Security Admission. Enforcement applies to new Pods: a Deployment whose template violates the standard is accepted, but its Replica Set cannot create Pods ( forbidden violates Pod Security ): read kube control describe rs. Module twelve shows the security Context settings that satisfy restricted.

1.title: ValidatingAdmissionPolicy
1.text: Validating Admission Policy. A Validating Admission Policy (stable A P I admissionregistration dot K eights dot io slash version one ) holds sell expressions, for example "every Deployment must have at least two replicas", and a Validating Admission Policy Binding says where it applies. A rejected request returns the policy's message. For the C K A D you only need to recognize it and read its error. Exam tip. "Forbidden" means authorization (R back): fix it with a Role and a Role Binding. "violates Pod Security" or "exceeded quota" or "maximum cpu usage" means admission: fix the object or the namespace setting, not R back. Exam tip. Test every R back change with kube control auth can i... the as flag set to system serviceaccount ns name for a yes and for a no that must stay no.

1.title: Lab 11.1: serviceaccount pod
1.text: Lab eleven point one: serviceaccount pod. This task is worth five points, and you should plan about five minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace auth, create a Service Account named app sa. Create a Pod named client (image busy box one dot thirty-six, command sleep three thousand six hundred ) that runs with that Service Account. Wait until it is Running. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

1.title: Lab 11.1: serviceaccount pod, Solution
1.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n auth create serviceaccount app sa. Then kube control dash n auth run client the image flag set to busy box one dot thirty-six the dry run flag set to client dash o yaml then the command sleep three thousand six, and so on. Then make the edit with sed, as shown on the screen. Then kube control apply dash f slash temp slash client dot yaml. Then kube control dash n auth wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash client the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n auth get pod client dash o json path dot spec dot service Account Name echo. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 11.2: no token automount
2.text: Lab eleven point two: no token automount. This task is worth six points, and you should plan about six minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace auth, the Service Account app sa exists. Create a Pod named quiet (image busy box one dot thirty-six, command sleep three thousand six hundred ) that runs with app sa but does not get an A P I token mounted into its containers (the directory slash var slash run slash secrets slash Kubernetes dot io slash serviceaccount must not exist in the container). Do this in the Pod, not by changing the Service Account. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 11.2: no token automount, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. kube control dash n auth apply dash f -. The manifest comes next, as shown on the screen. Then kube control dash n auth wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash quiet the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n auth exec quiet then the command ls slash var slash run slash secrets slash Kubernetes dot io slash serviceaccount then pipe to then pipe to echo no token directory. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 11.3: role rolebinding
2.text: Lab eleven point three: role rolebinding. This task is worth eight points, and you should plan about eight minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace auth, the Service Account app sa exists. Create a Role named pod reader that allows only get, list and watch on Pods, and a Role Binding named read pods that gives this Role to app sa. Afterwards the Service Account must be able to list Pods in auth but not delete them, and must not be able to list Pods in the namespace default. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 11.3: role rolebinding, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n auth create role pod reader the verb flag set to get,list,watch the resource flag set to pods. Then kube control dash n auth create rolebinding read pods the role flag set to pod reader the serviceaccount flag set to auth app sa. Then kube control dash n auth auth can i delete pods the as flag set to system serviceaccount auth app sa. Then kube control dash n auth auth can i list pods the as flag set to system serviceaccount auth app sa. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 11.4: clusterrole rolebinding
2.text: Lab eleven point four: clusterrole rolebinding. This task is worth seven points, and you should plan about seven minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. The Cluster Role deploy viewer (get and list on Deployments) already exists. In the namespace auth, give it to the Service Account app sa with a binding named view deploys, so that app sa can list Deployments in auth only. It must not be able to list Deployments in the namespace other. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 11.4: clusterrole rolebinding, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n auth create rolebinding view deploys the clusterrole flag set to deploy viewer the serviceaccount flag set to auth app sa. Then kube control dash n other auth can i list deployments the as flag set to system serviceaccount auth app sa. Then kube control dash n auth auth can i list deployments the as flag set to system serviceaccount auth app sa. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 11.5: create token
2.text: Lab eleven point five: create token. This task is worth five points, and you should plan about five minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace auth, the Service Account app sa exists. Create a token for it that is valid for exactly two hours, and write the token (just the token string) to about slash answers slash token dot txt on the host where you run kube control. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 11.5: create token, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n auth create token app sa the duration flag set to two hours about slash answers slash token dot txt. Then cut dash d. -f two about slash answers slash token dot txt then pipe to head dash c sixty echo. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 11.6: fix forbidden api call
2.text: Lab eleven point six: fix forbidden api call. This task is worth eight points, and you should plan about nine minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. In the namespace auth, the Pod caller (Service Account app sa ) asks the A P I server every three seconds for the list of Pods in its own namespace and prints the H T T P status code. It prints four hundred three. Without changing the Pod, give its Service Account exactly the access it needs, namely list on Pods in the namespace auth (use a Role named pod lister and a Role Binding named pod lister binding ), so that the log shows two hundred. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 11.6: fix forbidden api call, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control dash n auth logs caller then pipe to tail -two. Then kube control dash n auth create role pod lister the verb flag set to list the resource flag set to pods. Then kube control dash n auth create rolebinding pod lister binding the role flag set to pod lister the serviceaccount flag set to auth app sa. Then sleep six. Then kube control dash n auth logs caller then pipe to tail -two. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Lab 11.7: pod security admission
2.text: Lab eleven point seven: pod security admission. This task is worth seven points, and you should plan about seven minutes. Start by switching to the kind-ckad context. The namespace psa exists. Make the cluster reject Pods that violate the baseline Pod Security Standard in that namespace (enforce it with a namespace label, not just a warning). Then create a Pod named ok (image engine X alpine ), which must be accepted and Running. A privileged Pod must now be rejected in psa. Pause the video and try the task yourself, then come back for the solution.

2.title: Lab 11.7: pod security admission, Solution
2.text: Here is one way to solve it. Run kube control label namespace psa pod security dot Kubernetes dot io slash enforce baseline. Then kube control dash n psa run ok the image flag set to engine X alpine. Then kube control dash n psa wait the for flag set to condition Ready pod slash ok the timeout flag set to one hundred twenty seconds. Then kube control dash n psa apply dash f - Y echo rejected as expected. Then api Version version one. Then kind Pod. Then metadata name priv. Then spec. Then containers. The remaining lines are on the screen. Then check the result with a read command, the way you would on the exam.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What are the three gates of an A P I request, in order? Answer: Authentication, authorization, admission control. Question two. Which H T T P status means "not allowed" and which means "not authenticated"? Answer: four hundred three Forbidden is authorization; four hundred one Unauthorized is authentication. Question three. What identity does a Pod's Service Account have? Answer: system serviceaccount namespace name.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. How do you stop a Pod from receiving an A P I token? Answer: automount Service Account Token false in the Pod spec (or on the Service Account). Question five. What does a Role Binding that references a Cluster Role do? Answer: It grants the Cluster Role's rules only inside the binding's namespace. Question six. Which command shows whether a Service Account may delete Pods in a namespace? Answer: kube control auth can i delete pods dash n ns the as flag set to system serviceaccount ns name.

2.title: Recall Check 3
2.text: Recall check three. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question seven. What do the Pod Security labels enforce, warn and audit do? Answer: Enforce rejects violating Pods; warn shows a warning; audit records an audit annotation. Question eight. Can you create a deny rule in R back? Answer: No; R back only adds permissions.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Gates: authentication (four hundred one), authorization (four hundred three), admission (policy error). Service Account: service Account Name, token in slash var slash run slash secrets slash Kubernetes dot io slash serviceaccount, automount Service Account Token. Token: kube control create token sa the duration flag set to two hours. R back: Role or Cluster Role plus Role Binding or Cluster Role Binding; additive. Create: create role the verb flag the resource flag, create rolebinding the role flag (or the clusterrole flag ) the serviceaccount flag set to ns name. Test: kube control auth can i verb resource dash n ns the as flag set to... Admission: Service Account, Limit Ranger, Resource Quota, Pod Security, Validating Admission Policy, webhooks. Pod Security: namespace labels enforce slash warn slash audit with privileged slash baseline slash restricted.
